title: The Adani Group Just Cleared Its Biggest Legal Hurdle. Now Comes the $75-Billion Bet.
excerpt: With US criminal charges dismissed and stocks surging, Gautam Adani is deploying tens of thousands of crores across India — and the diaspora investors who held on are being vindicated
body:
## The Market's Verdict

It took less than 24 hours for Dalal Street to render its judgment. On the morning the US Department of Justice confirmed it had dropped all criminal charges against Gautam Adani and his nephew Sagar Adani, Adani Group stocks surged across the board — NDTV up over seven per cent, Adani Enterprises up five, Adani Green Energy up four. The Sensex and Nifty, which had spent weeks absorbing geopolitical shocks from the Middle East, found an unlikely booster in a federal courthouse in Brooklyn.

The DOJ's decision to dismiss the indictment "with prejudice" — meaning the charges cannot be refiled — closes a chapter that began in November 2024, when prosecutors alleged that Adani and his associates had paid $250 million in bribes to Indian officials to secure solar energy contracts. The Securities and Exchange Commission had simultaneously filed a civil case. That too has been settled: Adani Green Energy agreed to pay $275 million without admitting or denying the allegations.

## Anatomy of a Legal Unravelling

The criminal case collapsed for reasons that legal analysts say reflect prosecutorial overreach as much as any exoneration of the defendants. Jurisdictional challenges were cited: much of the alleged conduct occurred on Indian soil, between Indian companies and Indian officials, making a US prosecution legally fraught. The DOJ also reportedly struggled to secure cooperating witnesses willing to testify in an American courtroom about events in India.

For the Adani Group, the settlement arithmetic is straightforward. The combined cost — $275 million to the SEC, plus the Treasury's separate settlement over LPG import violations — amounts to roughly 0.5 per cent of the group's current market capitalisation. By any corporate standard, that is the cost of doing business, not an existential reckoning.

## From Courtroom to Construction Site

What has surprised market watchers is the speed with which Gautam Adani has pivoted from legal defence to capital deployment. In the week following the DOJ dismissal, the group announced a ₹60,000-crore investment push in Bihar, encompassing a 2,400 MW thermal power plant, smart meter installations, expanded cement production, and a ₹150-crore rural vision care initiative. In Assam, the figure is even larger: ₹63,000 crore in energy projects. The group's five-year energy transition commitment stands at $75 billion globally, with $10 billion earmarked for US energy and infrastructure projects — a pointed olive branch to the very country that had indicted its chairman.

The investment blitz serves a dual purpose. Domestically, it cements the Adani Group's role as a quasi-sovereign infrastructure partner — the company that builds ports, airports, power plants, and highways at a scale that few Indian conglomerates can match. Internationally, it signals that the legal cloud has lifted and that the group is open for business.

## The Diaspora Dividend

For the Indian diaspora, the Adani saga has always been more than a corporate story. The 2024 indictment was seen by many as a proxy for broader US-India tensions — a signal that Washington was willing to use its legal apparatus against Indian business interests. The dismissal, conversely, has been read as a de-escalation, one that may smooth the path for Indian conglomerates seeking capital and partnerships in Western markets.

NRI investors, who hold an estimated $15 billion in Indian equity portfolios, have been among the most vocal participants in the Adani debate. Those who bought during the post-indictment dip have been rewarded: Adani Enterprises is now trading above its pre-indictment levels. Those who sold have been left to contemplate the oldest lesson in Indian markets — that political risk, however severe it appears, rarely outweighs structural demand for infrastructure in a $4-trillion economy.

## What the Numbers Say

SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey's recent assertion that Indian markets are "resilient to West Asia shocks" applies doubly to the Adani saga. The group's combined market capitalisation has recovered to approximately $260 billion, from a post-indictment low of $150 billion. Gross debt remains elevated, but cash flows from operational ports, airports, and power plants provide a cushion that purely financial companies lack.

The legal saga is over. The infrastructure bet — and the political bet that undergirds it — is very much not.

*Sources: US Department of Justice court filing; SEC settlement documents; Outlook Business; Patna Press; India Tribune; Adani Group corporate disclosures.*
